The second reduction proves that the source has stopped decaying.

explanation: Paper is an effective absorber of alpha particles, while aluminium can absorb much of the beta radiation. Gamma rays are more penetrating, so they may still reach the detector. The readings support the presence of different radiations but do not, by themselves, establish exact source composition.

title: Understanding the operation of a radioactive tracer
question: </row> A detector records the passage of the tracer at different positions in a pipe. Why can a suitable radioactive tracer be useful for locating a blockage or measuring flow?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Tracer injected</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Flowing system</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Detector readings</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">A detector records the passage of the tracer at different positions in a pipe.</text></svg>

options.text: Its half-life increases when it enters the pipe.
It permanently changes the chemical identity of the entire fluid.
It makes the pipe transparent to visible light.
Its emitted radiation can be detected from outside suitable parts of the system, allowing the tracer's movement to be tracked.

explanation: A suitable tracer emits detectable radiation and can be followed through a system without requiring direct visual access. Its selection must consider the tracer's chemical behaviour, radiation type, half-life and safety. Option A is wrong because a substance's half-life is not increased merely by entering a pipe.

title: Interpreting carbon dating of an organic sample
question: </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> <row justify="center"> </row> Which assumption is essential to a simple carbon-dating interpretation?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Living organism         Carbon-14 continually replenished through exchange with the environment.</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Dead organism         Carbon exchange stops; carbon-14 decays.</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Measure remaining carbon-14 and compare with a suitable reference</text></svg>

options.text: Carbon-14 decays only when the sample is heated.
After death, the sample no longer replenishes its carbon-14 through biological exchange, and the initial ratio can be estimated appropriately.
Carbon-14 has the same mass number as carbon-12.
All carbon-14 disappears exactly after two half-lives.

explanation: Carbon dating relies on the reduction of carbon-14 after biological exchange ceases. The remaining carbon-14 is compared with an appropriate reference and the known half-life. Option D is incorrect: after two half-lives, one-quarter remains, not zero.

title: Identifying the role of control rods in an abnormal reactor condition
question: <row justify="center"> </row> <row justify="center"> </row> Which statement is correct if the reactor's chain reaction must be rapidly reduced?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">More neutrons remain available to sustain fission.</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">More neutrons are absorbed.</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Chain reaction rate decreases</text></svg>

options.text: Withdraw all control rods to increase neutron absorption.
Replace the moderator with fuel to ensure every neutron is absorbed.
Insert the control rods further so that more neutrons are absorbed, reducing the probability of further fission events.
Increase the fuel temperature indefinitely because temperature always stops fission.

explanation: Control rods absorb neutrons. Inserting them further reduces the neutron population available to sustain the chain reaction. The moderator's role is different: it slows neutrons rather than serving as the primary neutron-absorbing control mechanism.

title: Comparing energy release in nuclear and chemical reactions
question: </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> Both processes can release energy, but the changes occur at different levels of matter. Which statement best explains why nuclear reactions can release much more energy per event than ordinary chemical reactions?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Electronic rearrangement</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Nuclear transformation</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Both processes can release energy, but the changes occur at different levels of matter.</text></svg>

options.text: Nuclear reactions involve changes in the nucleus, whereas ordinary chemical reactions primarily involve electrons and chemical bonds.
Chemical reactions always absorb energy, whereas nuclear reactions always release it.
Nuclear reactions occur only in gases, whereas chemical reactions occur only in solids.
Nuclear reactions require no energy transfer, whereas chemical reactions require energy transfer.

explanation: Chemical reactions involve changes in electron arrangements and bonding; nuclear reactions involve transformations of nuclei. The energy scale associated with nuclear changes is generally much larger per event. Option B is false because chemical reactions can be exothermic or endothermic, and nuclear reactions can also require energy input.

title: Distinguishing a radioactive decay series from a sequence of chemical changes
question: <row align="center" justify="center" gap=> α emission </row> The diagram represents a change in the identity of the nucleus, not merely a change in electron arrangement. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{210}_{84}\mathrm{Po}\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">α emission</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{206}_{82}\mathrm{Pb}\,\)</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">The diagram represents a change in the identity of the nucleus, not merely a change in electron arrangement.</text></svg>

options.text: The daughter remains polonium because the number of electrons determines the element's identity.
The daughter is lead because alpha emission reduces the atomic number from 84 to 82.
The daughter is lead-210 because alpha particles carry no mass.
The daughter is bismuth because alpha emission increases the atomic number by two.

explanation:
The atomic number determines the element. Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons, changing polonium-210 into lead-206.


{}^{210}_{84}Po→
{}^{206}_{82}Pb+{}⁴_{2}He


Both mass number and atomic number balance. Option A confuses chemical changes with nuclear transmutation.

title: Identifying a safe shielding arrangement
question: </row> The shield reduces radiation reaching the worker, but the source remains radioactive. Which additional precaution is most appropriate when handling a radioactive source?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Radioactive source</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Lead shield</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Reduced exposure</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">The shield reduces radiation reaching the worker, but the source remains radioactive.</text></svg>

options.text: Hold the source directly to minimise the time spent moving it.
Remove the shielding whenever the source is not being measured.
Increase the exposure time to obtain a more reliable reading.
Minimise exposure time, maximise distance where practical, and use suitable shielding and handling equipment.

explanation: Radiation protection relies on reducing exposure time, increasing distance and using appropriate shielding. A shield does not necessarily eliminate all radiation, and the source remains radioactive even when not in use. Option B removes protection when it is not needed to do so.

title: Interpreting radioactive-waste storage
question: <row justify="center"> </row> <row justify="center"> </row> Why is simply burying all radioactive waste in an ordinary pit unacceptable?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Radioactive waste in a sealed, labelled container</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Shielded, secured storage with controlled access</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Monitoring and disposal according to authorised procedures</text></svg>

options.text: Every radioactive substance becomes harmless immediately after burial.
Radioactive decay stops completely underground.
Waste can contaminate the environment or expose people if containment, shielding, monitoring and disposal requirements are inadequate.
Radioactive waste emits only harmless visible light.

explanation: Radioactive waste must be managed according to its activity, half-life and other hazards. Improper disposal can allow radioactive materials to spread into soil or water or expose people to radiation. Burial does not stop radioactive decay, as option B suggests.

title: Identifying a chain reaction that becomes self-sustaining
question: <row justify="center"> </row> <row justify="center"> </row> <grid columns= gap=> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> The diagram shows the idealised branching pattern; in practice, some neutrons escape or are absorbed without causing fission. Which condition is necessary for a self-sustaining chain reaction?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">One neutron causes one fission</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Three neutrons are released</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Fission</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">The diagram shows the idealised branching pattern; in practice, some neutrons escape or are absorbed without causing fission.</text></svg>

options.text: Every neutron must escape from the fuel.
On average, enough neutrons from each generation must cause further fissions to maintain the reaction.
All neutrons must be absorbed by control rods.
The fuel must contain only non-radioactive nuclei.

explanation: A self-sustaining chain reaction requires sufficient neutrons from one generation of fissions to initiate further fissions. If too few do so, the reaction dies away; if too many cause additional fissions without control, the rate can increase. Option C would suppress rather than sustain the chain reaction.

title: Comparing a hydrogen bomb with a nuclear reactor
question: </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 142" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="122" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Heat is extracted for useful energy.</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Energy released extremely rapidly.</text></svg>

options.text: Both devices rely exclusively on chemical combustion.
A reactor and a hydrogen bomb must operate at identical temperatures and under identical control conditions.
A hydrogen bomb is an ordinary chemical explosive because hydrogen is a chemical element.
A hydrogen bomb uses nuclear fusion under extreme conditions, whereas a power reactor maintains a controlled nuclear chain reaction to produce useful energy.

explanation: Fusion requires extremely high temperatures and suitable conditions for light nuclei to combine. A power reactor normally uses a controlled fission chain reaction, with heat extracted for electricity generation. Option C incorrectly equates a nuclear reaction with chemical combustion.

title: Identifying radiation from electric-field deflection
question: Schematic: three beams enter a region between oppositely charged parallel plates. **Positive plate (+)** ──────────────── Beam enters → ──────────────── **Negative plate (−)** **Beam paths** α: curves ↓ β: curves ↑↑ γ: straight → Electric field points downward, from the positive upper plate to the negative lower plate. The figure labels the alpha path downward and the beta path upward. Which interpretation correctly explains all three paths?

explanation: An alpha particle has charge +2e, a beta-minus particle has charge -e, and gamma radiation has no electric charge. The electric field therefore deflects alpha downward and beta upward. options.text: Correct, because each half-life removes half the original nuclei.

A neutron in the nucleus transforms into a proton, producing an electron that is emitted as a beta-minus particle.

explanation:
correctly accounts for the transition shown?

A) A proton emits a gamma photon and becomes a neutron.

B) The nucleus emits an alpha particle followed by a gamma photon.

C) A neutron in the nucleus transforms into a proton, producing an electron that is emitted as a beta-minus particle.

D) An electron already orbiting the atom is expelled, increasing the nuclear atomic number.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** In beta-minus decay, a neutron transforms into a proton and an electron is emitted. The daughter has one additional proton but the same total number of nucleons.

Option D confuses orbital electrons with beta particles created during a nuclear transformation.

Smoke causes alpha particles to acquire a large positive charge.

explanation:
correctly describes the operating principle?

A) Alpha particles detect smoke by reflecting from every smoke particle like visible light.

B) Smoke causes alpha particles to acquire a large positive charge.

C) Smoke increases the nuclear half-life of the source, lowering its activity.

explanation:
correctly accounts for the transition shown?

A) A proton emits a gamma photon and becomes a neutron.

B) The nucleus emits an alpha particle followed by a gamma photon.

C) A neutron in the nucleus transforms into a proton, producing an electron that is emitted as a beta-minus particle.

D) An electron already orbiting the atom is expelled, increasing the nuclear atomic number.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** In beta-minus decay, a neutron transforms into a proton and an electron is emitted. The daughter has one additional proton but the same total number of nucleons.

Option D confuses orbital electrons with beta particles created during a nuclear transformation.

question: </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> Each box gives the mass number above the atomic number. Which comparison is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Nuclide P         \(\,{}^{14}_{6}\mathrm C\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Nuclide Q         \(\,{}^{12}_{6}\mathrm C\,\)</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Nuclide R         \(\,{}^{14}_{7}\mathrm N\,\)</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Each box gives the mass number above the atomic number.</text></svg>

options.text: P and R are isotopes because their mass numbers are equal.
P and Q are isotopes because they have the same atomic number but different mass numbers; P and R are isobars.
Q and R are isotones because they have the same atomic number.
All three nuclides are isotopes of carbon.

explanation: P and Q are both carbon nuclei with Z=6, but their mass numbers are 14 and 12. P and R both have A=14 but different atomic numbers, making them isobars. Their neutron numbers are also different: P has 8 and R has 7. Option A confuses isobars with isotopes.

title: Interpreting a radioactive source and detector arrangement
question: </row> Reading without absorber: 900 counts/min. Reading with absorber X: 120 counts/min. Background: 20 counts/min. What fraction of the original net detected count rate remains after inserting absorber X?

Reading with absorber X: 120 counts/min. Background: 20 counts/min.</text></svg>
explanation:
Subtract background before comparing the rates.

- Initial net rate =900-20=880 counts/min.
- Final net rate =120-20=100 counts/min.
- Fraction remaining =100/880=5/44.

**Correction check:** The exact fraction is (5 / 44), which is not among the listed options. Therefore, the question as drawn is invalid. A rigorous examiner must not force a false answer. For this question, the intended concept is background correction; the options must be repaired before use.

title: Reading alpha decay from a two-stage diagram
question: <row justify="center"> </row> <row justify="center"> </row> Both arrows represent separate emissions; neither emitted particle is shown. Which statement describes the two transitions correctly?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}\,\)</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}\,\)</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Both arrows represent separate emissions; neither emitted particle is shown.</text></svg>

options.text: Both are beta-minus emissions because the atomic number decreases.
The first is alpha emission and the second is beta-minus emission.
Each transition is an alpha emission, so the total decrease in mass number is 8 and in atomic number is 4.
The first is gamma emission and the second is alpha emission.

explanation: Each step reduces A by 4 and Z by 2. Both are alpha decays. Across the complete chain, the mass number falls from 226 to 218 and the atomic number from 88 to 84.

title: Determining the missing daughter in a nuclear equation
question: </row> Which nuclide completes the equation?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{210}_{84}\mathrm{Po}\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Daughter nucleus</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\,\)</text></svg>
explanation:
Subtract the emitted alpha particle's numbers from those of the parent:


A=210-4=206,qquad Z=84-2=82.


The daughter is lead-206, ,{}^{206}_{82}Pb. Option C subtracts the mass number but incorrectly retains the original atomic number.

title: Interpreting a half-life experiment
question: A student concludes that the sample loses 400 Bq during every five-minute interval. Which interpretation is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 94" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="10" width="430" height="74" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="15" y="10" width="430" height="37" rx="6" fill="#f1f5f9"/><line x1="15" y1="47" x2="445" y2="47" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="30" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">Time (min)</text><text x="114" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">0</text><text x="198" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">5</text><text x="282" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">10</text><text x="366" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">15</text><rect x="16" y="52" width="428" height="32" fill="#fafafa"/><text x="30" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">Net activity (Bq)</text><text x="114" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">800</text><text x="198" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">400</text><text x="282" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">200</text><text x="366" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">100</text></svg>

options.text: The conclusion is correct because the half-life is five minutes.
The activity decreases by a constant fraction, not a constant absolute amount; the half-life is five minutes.
The half-life increases from five to ten minutes as the activity falls.
The sample becomes non-radioactive after 15 minutes.

explanation: The successive decreases are 400, 200 and 100 Bq. Each decrease is half the activity at the beginning of its interval. The half-life is constant at five minutes; option A confuses a constant half-life with a constant absolute decrease.

title: Distinguishing gamma emission from a nuclear transmutation
question: <row justify="center"> </row> A wavy arrow leaves the nucleus and is labelled γ. Which statement follows from the diagram?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Excited nucleus     \(\,{}^{60}_{27}\mathrm{Co}^{*}\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Lower-energy nucleus     \(\,{}^{60}_{27}\mathrm{Co}\,\)</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">A wavy arrow leaves the nucleus and is labelled γ.</text></svg>

options.text: The nucleus loses two protons and two neutrons.
The nucleus gains one proton because gamma radiation is positively charged.
The nucleus's atomic number decreases while its mass number remains unchanged.
The nucleus loses energy, but its atomic number and mass number remain unchanged.

explanation: Gamma emission releases excess nuclear energy as an electromagnetic wave. It does not change the number of protons or nucleons. Options A and C describe changes associated with particle emission, not gamma emission.

title: Analysing a fission chain-reaction diagram
question: <row justify="center"> </row> <row justify="center" gap=> </row> <grid columns= gap=> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> If each fission event releases three neutrons, why does a reactor not necessarily undergo an uncontrolled explosion?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 198" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="178" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Neutron + \(\,{}^{235}_{92}\mathrm U\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Fission fragments + 3 neutrons + energy</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Further fission</text></svg>

options.text: The moderator absorbs all neutrons before they can cause fission.
Control rods absorb excess neutrons so that the chain reaction can be maintained at a controlled rate.
Fission neutrons have no effect on other uranium nuclei.
The coolant converts neutrons into gamma rays, stopping every subsequent fission.

explanation: A controlled reactor regulates the neutron population using neutron-absorbing control rods. The moderator slows fast neutrons to improve the probability of further fission in a suitable reactor. Option A confuses the moderator's principal role with the control rods' role.

title: Identifying the function of components in a nuclear reactor
question: </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> Which component-function pairing is incorrectly stated?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Uranium fuel</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Neutron-absorbing material</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Slows neutrons</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Carries heat away</text></svg>

options.text: A — supplies nuclei that undergo fission.
B — regulates the chain reaction by absorbing neutrons.
C — slows neutrons, increasing the chance of fission in a suitable reactor.
D — slows neutrons and is always the principal neutron moderator.

explanation: The coolant primarily transfers heat away from the reactor core. A coolant may also act as a moderator in some reactor designs, but it is not necessarily the moderator or always the principal moderator. The other three pairings describe the standard qualitative functions correctly.

title: Interpreting a fusion diagram
question: </row> <row justify="center"> </row> The reactants are forced close together under extremely high temperature and suitable pressure conditions. Which statement correctly explains the process?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Light nucleus       \(\,{}^{2}_{1}\mathrm H\,\)</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Light nucleus       \(\,{}^{3}_{1}\mathrm H\,\)</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">\(\,{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\,\) + \(\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm n\,\) + energy</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">The reactants are forced close together under extremely high temperature and suitable pressure conditions.</text></svg>

options.text: It is fusion because two light nuclei combine to produce a heavier nucleus and a neutron, releasing energy.
It is fission because a helium nucleus splits into hydrogen nuclei.
It is chemical combustion because no nuclear identity changes.
It is alpha decay because the helium nucleus is emitted by a heavy parent nucleus.

explanation: The nuclear equation balances: mass numbers 2+3=4+1, and atomic numbers 1+1=2+0. Two light nuclei combine, so this is nuclear fusion. Option D incorrectly labels a reaction between two light reactants as alpha decay.

title: Understanding a thickness gauge
question: </row> Sheet becomes thicker → detector count rate decreases, with source strength and other conditions held constant. The detector reading falls below the calibrated range. Which conclusion and corrective action are most appropriate?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Beta source</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Moving sheet</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Detector</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Sheet becomes thicker → detector count rate decreases, with source strength and other conditions held constant.</text></svg>

options.text: The sheet must be thinner; move the source farther away to increase absorption.
The beta source has necessarily stopped emitting radiation; replace it immediately.
The sheet may be too thick for the calibrated operating range; reduce the thickness or adjust the gauge's calibrated operating arrangement.
The reading proves that the sheet has become radioactive.

explanation: A thickness gauge infers sheet thickness from the radiation reaching the detector. A thicker sheet generally absorbs more beta radiation, reducing the detector count rate. A very low reading may be outside the calibration range; it does not by itself prove source failure or induced radioactivity.

title: Distinguishing natural radioactivity from induced radioactivity
question: </grid-item> <grid-item> </grid-item> </grid> Which classification is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 142" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="122" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Emits radiation without deliberate irradiation</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Bombarded with neutrons, producing a radioactive nuclide</text></svg>

options.text: X and Y both demonstrate only natural radioactivity because neutrons occur naturally.
X illustrates natural radioactivity, while Y illustrates artificial radioactivity produced by nuclear bombardment.
X illustrates artificial radioactivity because uranium is a heavy element.
Y cannot become radioactive unless electrons are added to the target atom.

explanation: Natural radioactivity occurs spontaneously in unstable nuclei found in nature. Artificial radioactivity can be produced by bombarding a suitable stable nucleus with particles such as neutrons. Option A confuses the possible natural occurrence of neutrons with the deliberate production of a radioactive nuclide.

title: Determining the role of a moderator from neutron paths
question: </row> <row justify="center"> </row> A student argues that because the moderator slows neutrons, it must stop the chain reaction. Which statement best evaluates this argument?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 254" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="440" height="234" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="25" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="47" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Fast neutron</text><path d="M230 63 L230 75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,74 234,74 230,80" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="81" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Moderator</text><path d="M230 119 L230 131" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,130 234,130 230,136" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="137" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Slower neutron</text><path d="M230 175 L230 187" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="226,186 234,186 230,192" fill="#64748b"/><rect x="40" y="193" width="380" height="36" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="230" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#1e293b">Increased chance of fission in a suitable thermal reactor</text></svg>

options.text: Correct; slower neutrons cannot cause fission in any material.
Correct; slowing neutrons is exactly the same as absorbing them completely.
Incorrect; a suitable moderator slows neutrons without necessarily absorbing them, and slower neutrons can be more effective at causing fission in a suitable reactor.
Incorrect; the moderator's primary function is to cool the fuel and remove all fission products.

explanation: Moderation reduces neutron speed through collisions, while control rods regulate the chain reaction by absorbing neutrons. In suitable reactors using fissile fuel such as uranium-235, slower neutrons can have a higher probability of causing fission. Option B confuses reducing neutron energy with removing neutrons from the reaction.

title: Deflection in Perpendicular Magnetic Field (Into the Page)
question: A radioactive source inside a thick lead block emits three distinct radiations (X, Y, and Z) directed vertically upward into a uniform magnetic field pointing perpendicularly into the plane of paper (indicated by ⊗). Based on the observed trajectories shown in the diagram, identify the three radiations X, Y, and Z and explain the direction of deflection using Fleming's Left Hand Rule.
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="135" y="160" width="90" height="42" fill="#64748b" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2" rx="3"/>
  <rect x="165" y="160" width="30" height="24" fill="#0f172a"/>
  <circle cx="180" cy="175" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/>
  <text x="145" y="196" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#f8fafc">Lead Collimator</text>
  <!-- Magnetic field area markers -->
  <g fill="#94a3b8" font-size="12" font-family="monospace">
    <text x="50" y="50">⊗</text><text x="110" y="50">⊗</text><text x="180" y="50">⊗</text><text x="250" y="50">⊗</text><text x="310" y="50">⊗</text>
    <text x="50" y="95">⊗</text><text x="110" y="95">⊗</text><text x="180" y="95">⊗</text><text x="250" y="95">⊗</text><text x="310" y="95">⊗</text>
    <text x="50" y="140">⊗</text><text x="110" y="140">⊗</text><text x="180" y="140">⊗</text><text x="250" y="140">⊗</text><text x="310" y="140">⊗</text>
  </g>
  <text x="235" y="32" font-size="11" font-weight="600" fill="#475569">B (into paper ⊗)</text>
  <!-- Undeflected Y beam (Gamma) -->
  <line x1="180" y1="160" x2="180" y2="25" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polygon points="180,18 176,27 184,27" fill="#16a34a"/>
  <text x="186" y="24" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Beam Y</text>
  <!-- Gentle Left Deflection X beam (Alpha) -->
  <path d="M 180 160 Q 180 100 110 50" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polygon points="104,46 112,54 116,46" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <text x="75" y="44" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">Beam X</text>
  <!-- Sharp Right Deflection Z beam (Beta) -->
  <path d="M 180 160 Q 180 115 260 85" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polygon points="266,82 256,86 261,93" fill="#2563eb"/>
  <text x="272" y="86" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">Beam Z</text>
</svg>

options.text: X = α-particles, Y = γ-rays, Z = β-particles
X = β-particles, Y = γ-rays, Z = α-particles
X = α-particles, Y = β-particles, Z = γ-rays
X = γ-rays, Y = α-particles, Z = β-particles

explanation: By Fleming's Left Hand Rule: Forefinger points into paper (B ⊗), middle finger points in the direction of conventional current (upward for positive charge). The thumb points towards the LEFT, so positively charged α-particles deflect to the left (Beam X). Negatively charged β-particles deflect in the opposite direction (to the right) with a much sharper curvature due to their extremely small mass (Beam Z). Neutral γ-rays experience no magnetic Lorentz force (q = 0) and pass undeflected (Beam Y).
concept_name: Deflection of α, β, and γ in Magnetic Fields

title: Deflection in Electrostatic Field Between Charged Parallel Plates
question: A collimated beam of radiation from a radioactive sample enters horizontally between two charged metal plates as illustrated. Beam P curves toward the upper plate (+), Beam Q continues straight without deviation, and Beam R curves gently toward the lower plate (-). Why does Beam P exhibit significantly greater curvature than Beam R despite having a smaller magnitude of charge than the alpha particle?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Top Plate (+) -->
  <rect x="90" y="30" width="180" height="12" fill="#ef4444" rx="2"/>
  <text x="100" y="24" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#ef4444">+ + + + + + Positive Plate (+V) + + + + + +</text>
  <!-- Bottom Plate (-) -->
  <rect x="90" y="155" width="180" height="12" fill="#3b82f6" rx="2"/>
  <text x="96" y="180" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#3b82f6">- - - - - - Negative Plate (-V) - - - - - -</text>
  <!-- Collimator Source -->
  <rect x="15" y="80" width="45" height="35" fill="#475569" rx="3"/>
  <circle cx="35" cy="97" r="4" fill="#fbbf24"/>
  <!-- Fluorescent Screen on Right -->
  <rect x="320" y="20" width="10" height="160" fill="#cbd5e1" stroke="#94a3b8" rx="2"/>
  <text x="334" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b" transform="rotate(90,334,105)">SCREEN</text>
  <!-- Beam P (Beta -> +) -->
  <path d="M 60 97 Q 160 97 320 48" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <circle cx="320" cy="48" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/>
  <text x="260" y="42" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">Beam P (β⁻)</text>
  <!-- Beam Q (Gamma -> straight) -->
  <line x1="60" y1="97" x2="320" y2="97" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <circle cx="320" cy="97" r="4" fill="#16a34a"/>
  <text x="260" y="92" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Beam Q (γ)</text>
  <!-- Beam R (Alpha -> -) -->
  <path d="M 60 97 Q 170 97 320 135" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <circle cx="320" cy="135" r="4" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <text x="260" y="148" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">Beam R (α)</text>
</svg>

options.text: Beta particles have a much higher specific charge (charge-to-mass ratio e/m) because their mass is roughly 1/7340 times the mass of an alpha particle.
Beta particles carry twice the electrical charge of alpha particles.
Alpha particles travel at the speed of light, so the electric field has no time to deflect them.
The positive plate attracts electrons with a stronger gravitational force.

explanation: Transverse acceleration in an electric field is given by a = qE/m. The deflection curvature is directly proportional to the specific charge (q/m). For an electron (β-particle), (e/m)_β is approximately 7340/2 ≈ 3670 times greater than that of an alpha particle ((2e)/(4u)). Hence, despite having only half the charge of an alpha particle, its minuscule mass produces an enormous acceleration, causing Beam P to curve far more sharply toward the positive plate.

title: Radioactive Decay Series on A vs Z Coordinate Plane
question: The graph shows a nuclear decay sequence starting from nucleus P(Z=92, A=238) to nucleus S. Transition 1 goes from P to Q, Transition 2 from Q to R, and Transition 3 from R to S. Identify the radiations emitted in steps 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and determine the atomic number (Z) and mass number (A) of nucleus S.

options.text: Step 1: α, Step 2: β, Step 3: β; Nucleus S has Z = 92, A = 234 (an isotope of P)
Step 1: β, Step 2: α, Step 3: γ; Nucleus S has Z = 91, A = 230
Step 1: α, Step 2: α, Step 3: β; Nucleus S has Z = 89, A = 230
Step 1: γ, Step 2: β, Step 3: α; Nucleus S has Z = 90, A = 234

explanation:
Step 1 reduces mass number A from 238 to 234 (ΔA = -4) and atomic number Z from 92 to 90 (ΔZ = -2), which is an alpha (α) emission: ²³⁸₉₂P → ²³⁴₉₀Q + ⁴₂He.
Step 2 keeps A constant (234) while Z increases from 90 to 91 (ΔZ = +1), characteristic of beta (β⁻) emission: ²³⁴₉₀Q → ²³⁴₉₁R + ⁰₋₁e.
Step 3 also keeps A = 234 while Z increases from 91 to 92 (ΔZ = +1), another beta (β⁻) emission: ²³⁴₉₁R → ²³⁴₉₂S + ⁰₋₁e.
Final nucleus S has Z = 92 and A = 234. Since P and S both have Z = 92, they are isotopes of Uranium (²³⁸U and ²³⁴U).
concept_name: Nuclear Decay Chains and Isotope Formation

title: Activity-Time Decay Curve Analysis
question: The graph illustrates the radioactive decay curve of a newly synthesized radioisotope, plotting activity (in Becquerels) against time (in hours). Using the data from the graph, determine the half-life of the radioisotope and find its expected activity at t = 36 hours.
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Axes -->
  <line x1="60" y1="175" x2="330" y2="175" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="330,175 322,171 322,179" fill="#334155"/>
  <text x="160" y="196" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Time (hours) →</text>
  <line x1="60" y1="175" x2="60" y2="20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="60,20 56,28 64,28" fill="#334155"/>
  <text x="14" y="115" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#334155" transform="rotate(-90,14,115)">Activity (Bq) →</text>
  <!-- Grid markings -->
  <text x="25" y="38" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">800</text><line x1="56" y1="35" x2="60" y2="35" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <text x="25" y="73" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">400</text><line x1="56" y1="70" x2="60" y2="70" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <text x="25" y="108" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">200</text><line x1="56" y1="105" x2="60" y2="105" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <text x="25" y="143" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">100</text><line x1="56" y1="140" x2="60" y2="140" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <text x="120" y="188" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">12</text><line x1="125" y1="175" x2="125" y2="179" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <text x="185" y="188" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">24</text><line x1="190" y1="175" x2="190" y2="179" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <text x="250" y="188" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">36</text><line x1="255" y1="175" x2="255" y2="179" stroke="#64748b"/>
  <!-- Dashed guideline to T1/2 = 12h -->
  <line x1="60" y1="70" x2="125" y2="70" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <line x1="125" y1="70" x2="125" y2="175" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <circle cx="125" cy="70" r="3.5" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <!-- Dashed guideline to 24h -->
  <line x1="60" y1="105" x2="190" y2="105" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <line x1="190" y1="105" x2="190" y2="175" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <circle cx="190" cy="105" r="3.5" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <!-- Decay Curve -->
  <path d="M 60 35 Q 90 60 125 70 T 190 105 T 255 140 T 310 162" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <circle cx="60" cy="35" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/>
  <circle cx="255" cy="140" r="3.5" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <text x="135" y="65" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">(12 h, 400 Bq)</text>
  <text x="200" y="100" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">(24 h, 200 Bq)</text>
</svg>

options.text: Half-life = 12 hours; Activity at 36 h = 100 Bq
Half-life = 6 hours; Activity at 36 h = 50 Bq
Half-life = 24 hours; Activity at 36 h = 200 Bq
Half-life = 12 hours; Activity at 36 h = 50 Bq

explanation:
At t = 0, initial activity A₀ = 800 Bq.
Half of initial activity is 400 Bq, which occurs exactly at t = 12 hours. Therefore, the half-life T₁/₂ = 12 hours.
At t = 24 hours (2 half-lives), activity drops to 400/2 = 200 Bq.
At t = 36 hours (3 half-lives), activity drops to 200/2 = 100 Bq (or A = A₀ × (1/2)³ = 800 / 8 = 100 Bq).
concept_name: Half-life Calculation from Radioactive Decay Graphs

title: Penetrating Power and Multi-Stage Absorber Test
question: A mixed radioactive beam containing alpha, beta, and gamma emissions passes sequentially through three barriers: Sheet 1 (0.1 mm paper), Sheet 2 (5 mm aluminium), and Block 3 (10 cm lead). GM counter detectors D1, D2, and D3 measure the transmitted radiations after each barrier. Which of the following correctly describes what reaches detectors D1, D2, and D3?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Source -->
  <rect x="15" y="80" width="30" height="40" fill="#475569" rx="2"/>
  <circle cx="30" cy="100" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/>
  <text x="10" y="135" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#475569">Source (α,β,γ)</text>
  <!-- Barrier 1: Paper -->
  <rect x="100" y="45" width="4" height="110" fill="#f87171"/>
  <text x="80" y="38" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#b91c1c">Paper (0.1 mm)</text>
  <rect x="130" y="70" width="22" height="60" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#64748b" rx="2"/>
  <text x="133" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">D₁</text>
  <!-- Barrier 2: Aluminium -->
  <rect x="185" y="45" width="12" height="110" fill="#60a5fa"/>
  <text x="165" y="38" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1d4ed8">Al (5 mm)</text>
  <rect x="225" y="70" width="22" height="60" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#64748b" rx="2"/>
  <text x="228" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">D₂</text>
  <!-- Barrier 3: Thick Lead -->
  <rect x="275" y="45" width="25" height="110" fill="#94a3b8"/>
  <text x="260" y="38" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Lead (10 cm)</text>
  <rect x="325" y="70" width="22" height="60" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#64748b" rx="2"/>
  <text x="328" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">D₃</text>
  <!-- Alpha stopped at Paper -->
  <line x1="45" y1="85" x2="98" y2="85" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="50" y="80" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">α (stopped)</text>
  <!-- Beta passes paper, stopped at Al -->
  <line x1="45" y1="100" x2="183" y2="100" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
  <!-- Gamma passes paper and Al, heavily attenuated at Lead -->
  <line x1="45" y1="115" x2="273" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/>
</svg>

options.text: D1 detects β and γ; D2 detects only γ; D3 detects practically negligible radiation (or highly attenuated γ)
D1 detects α, β, and γ; D2 detects β; D3 detects α
D1 detects only α; D2 detects only β; D3 detects only γ
D1 detects only γ; D2 detects β and γ; D3 detects α and β

explanation:
Alpha particles have the lowest penetrating power (~0.04 mm in human tissue) and are completely stopped by a thin sheet of paper (0.1 mm). Thus, only β and γ reach detector D1.
Beta particles can penetrate paper but are completely absorbed by ~5 mm of aluminium. Therefore, only γ-radiation passes through Sheet 2 to reach detector D2.
Gamma radiation has immense penetrating power but is exponentially attenuated by dense lead; 10 cm of lead absorbs roughly 99%+ of the γ photons, leaving minimal intensity at D3.

title: Magnetic Field Directed Out of the Plane (⊙)
question: A radioactive beam travels vertically upward into a region of uniform magnetic field acting perpendicularly OUT of the page (represented by ⊙). Beam 1 deflects to the right, Beam 2 goes straight, and Beam 3 deflects to the left. Applying Fleming's Left Hand Rule, identify the radiations corresponding to Beams 1, 2, and 3.

options.text: Beam 1 = α-particles, Beam 2 = γ-rays, Beam 3 = β-particles
Beam 1 = β-particles, Beam 2 = γ-rays, Beam 3 = α-particles
Beam 1 = γ-rays, Beam 2 = α-particles, Beam 3 = β-particles
Beam 1 = α-particles, Beam 2 = β-particles, Beam 3 = γ-rays

explanation: For magnetic field directed OUT of the paper (⊙): Align your left hand such that the forefinger points outwards (towards you), and the middle finger points upward (direction of positive current). The thumb naturally points to the RIGHT. Hence, positively charged α-particles experience a magnetic Lorentz force towards the right (Beam 1). Negatively charged β-particles deflect in the opposite direction, i.e., towards the left, with greater curvature (Beam 3). Photons (γ-rays) carry zero net charge and pass straight undeflected (Beam 2).
concept_name: Lorentz Force Inversion with Magnetic Field Orientation

title: Nuclear Fission Reaction of Uranium-235
question: The diagram depicts the thermal neutron-induced fission of a Uranium-235 nucleus: ¹₀n + ²³⁵₉₂U → ²³⁶₉₂U* → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x (¹₀n) + Q What is the value of x (number of prompt neutrons released) and approximately how much energy Q is liberated per single fission event?

  <circle cx="285" cy="85" r="4" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="294" y="88" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#3b82f6">¹₀n</text>
  <line x1="205" y1="95" x2="280" y2="98" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="2,2"/>
  <circle cx="285" cy="98" r="4" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="294" y="101" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#3b82f6">¹₀n</text>
  <line x1="205" y1="95" x2="280" y2="111" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="2,2"/>
  <circle cx="285" cy="111" r="4" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="294" y="114" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#3b82f6">¹₀n</text>
  <!-- Energy burst -->
  <text x="260" y="180" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626">+ Energy (Q)</text>
</svg>

options.text: x = 3 neutrons; Q ≈ 200 MeV
x = 2 neutrons; Q ≈ 20 MeV
x = 1 neutron; Q ≈ 931 MeV
x = 4 neutrons; Q ≈ 0.51 MeV

explanation:
By conservation of nucleon number (mass number A):
Total Initial A = 1 + 235 = 236.
Total Final A = 141 (Ba) + 92 (Kr) + x(1) = 233 + x.
Equating: 236 = 233 + x ⟹ x = 3 neutrons.
Conservation of atomic number (Z): 0 + 92 = 56 + 36 + x(0) = 92 (balanced).
The mass defect between the reactants and fission fragments equals approx 0.215 u, which releases Q ≈ 0.215 × 931.5 MeV ≈ 200 MeV of energy primarily as kinetic energy of fission fragments.

title: Electrostatic Field with Inverted Polarity
question: In an electrostatic deflection chamber, the upper plate is maintained at negative potential (-V) and the lower plate at positive potential (+V). A narrow beam of radiation from a radium source enters the space between the plates. Towards which plate will the alpha (α) particles and beta (β) particles deflect?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Top Plate (-) -->
  <rect x="80" y="30" width="180" height="10" fill="#3b82f6" rx="2"/>
  <text x="96" y="24" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#3b82f6">- - - - - - Negative Plate (-V) - - - - - -</text>
  <!-- Bottom Plate (+) -->
  <rect x="80" y="150" width="180" height="10" fill="#ef4444" rx="2"/>
  <text x="96" y="174" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#ef4444">+ + + + + + Positive Plate (+V) + + + + + +</text>
  <!-- Source -->
  <rect x="15" y="80" width="40" height="30" fill="#475569" rx="2"/>
  <circle cx="35" cy="95" r="4" fill="#fbbf24"/>
  <!-- Screen -->
  <rect x="310" y="25" width="8" height="140" fill="#94a3b8" rx="2"/>
  <!-- Alpha towards Negative (Upward) -->
  <path d="M 55 95 Q 155 95 310 60" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text x="250" y="52" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">Track 1</text>
  <!-- Gamma Straight -->
  <line x1="55" y1="95" x2="310" y2="95" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text x="250" y="90" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Track 2</text>
  <!-- Beta towards Positive (Downward) -->
  <path d="M 55 95 Q 155 95 310 145" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text x="250" y="140" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">Track 3</text>
</svg>

options.text: Alpha deflects to Track 1 (towards upper negative plate); Beta deflects to Track 3 (towards lower positive plate); Gamma is Track 2
Alpha deflects to Track 3; Beta deflects to Track 1; Gamma is Track 2
Alpha and Beta both deflect to Track 1
Alpha deflects to Track 2; Beta deflects to Track 3

explanation:
Because the electrostatic polarity is inverted (top plate is negative and bottom plate is positive), the electrostatic force F = qE acts as follows:
- Alpha particles carry positive charge (+2e) and are attracted upward towards the negative plate (Track 1).
- Beta particles carry negative charge (-e) and are attracted downward towards the positive plate (Track 3) with larger curvature due to tiny mass.
- Gamma rays carry zero charge and proceed along Track 2 without deflection.
concept_name: Electrostatic Field Polarity and Charge Identification

title: Lead Container Collimation and Radiation Safety
question: A cross-section of a laboratory lead castle is shown. The radioactive pellet is placed at the bottom of a deep, narrow cavity in a lead box whose walls are at least 10 cm thick. What are the two primary physical reasons for using thick lead with a narrow channel?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

  <rect x="160" y="30" width="40" height="110" fill="#fffcf7" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/>
  <!-- Radioactive Source Pellet -->
  <circle cx="180" cy="125" r="9" fill="#ef4444" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="135" y="165" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Pellet at Bottom</text>
  <!-- Collimated Beam Emitting Out -->
  <line x1="180" y1="115" x2="180" y2="10" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="3,2"/>
  <polygon points="180,5 174,15 186,15" fill="#f59e0b"/>
  <text x="195" y="20" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#d97706">Collimated Beam</text>
  <!-- Dimension indicators -->
  <line x1="70" y1="100" x2="160" y2="100" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="80" y="93" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Wall ≥ 10 cm</text>
</svg>

options.text: Lead has high density and high atomic number (Z=82) to effectively absorb stray gamma rays, while the narrow channel collimates the rays into a fine parallel beam.
Lead neutralizes the radioactivity by chemical reaction with Uranium.
The thick lead speeds up alpha particles so they can be studied.
Lead acts as a magnetic shield that completely prevents all nuclear decay.

explanation: Lead (Pb, Z = 82) is chosen because of its exceptionally high density (11.3 g/cm³) and large atomic number, which maximize photon absorption via the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. A thickness of ≥ 10 cm absorbs almost all harmful stray gamma radiation, protecting personnel. The deep, narrow cavity allows only those rays directed straight up along the axis to emerge, providing a narrow, collimated pencil beam essential for precision experiments.

title: Binding Energy Per Nucleon Curve and Nuclear Stability
question: The graph outlines the Binding Energy per Nucleon (B.E./A) as a function of Mass Number (A). The curve peaks at Iron-56 (approx 8.8 MeV/nucleon) and drops for heavier nuclei (approx 7.6 MeV/nucleon at Uranium-238). Based on this curve, why do very heavy nuclei (e.g. U-235) undergo nuclear fission, while very light nuclei (e.g. Deuterium and Tritium) undergo nuclear fusion?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>

  <line x1="50" y1="180" x2="330" y2="180" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="330,180 322,176 322,184" fill="#334155"/>
  <text x="160" y="200" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Mass Number (A) →</text>
  <line x1="50" y1="180" x2="50" y2="20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="50,20 46,28 54,28" fill="#334155"/>
  <text x="14" y="115" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#334155" transform="rotate(-90,14,115)">B.E. / Nucleon (MeV) →</text>
  <!-- Peak at Fe-56 -->
  <circle cx="120" cy="45" r="4" fill="#ef4444"/>
  <text x="105" y="38" font-size="10" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626">⁵⁶Fe (8.8 MeV)</text>
  <!-- Light nuclei (Fusion region) -->
  <text x="58" y="145" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">²H, ³H</text>
  <path d="M 65 140 Q 90 90 120 45" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="55" y="105" font-size="9" font-weight="800" fill="#2563eb">Fusion →</text>
  <!-- Heavy nuclei (Fission region) -->
  <path d="M 120 45 Q 220 55 310 75" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <circle cx="310" cy="75" r="4" fill="#d97706"/>
  <text x="280" y="95" font-size="9" font-weight="800" fill="#d97706">²³⁸U (7.6 MeV)</text>
  <text x="210" y="80" font-size="9" font-weight="800" fill="#d97706">← Fission</text>
</svg>

options.text: Both processes move product nuclei toward the higher binding energy peak near Fe-56, resulting in a positive mass defect and huge energy release.
Fission only occurs when nuclei have zero binding energy.
Light nuclei have higher binding energy than Iron, so they break apart.
Heavy nuclei undergo fusion to become even heavier and more radioactive.

explanation:
The peak of the curve around A ≈ 56 (Iron/Nickel) represents the most tightly bound and stable nuclei with ~8.8 MeV/nucleon.
1. When two light nuclei fuse (A < 20), the resulting nucleus has a significantly higher binding energy per nucleon, converting lost mass into fusion energy.
2. When a heavy nucleus (A ≈ 235, B.E./A ≈ 7.6 MeV) splits into mid-sized fragments (A ≈ 100-140, B.E./A ≈ 8.5 MeV), the fragments are more tightly bound, releasing ~0.9 MeV per nucleon (total ~200 MeV per fission event).
concept_name: Nuclear Stability and Binding Energy Curve

title: Conservation of Linear Momentum in Alpha Decay
question: A stationary Radium nucleus (²²⁶₈₈Ra) at rest disintegrates via alpha emission into a Radon nucleus (²²²₈₆Rn) and an alpha particle (⁴₂He): ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He By conservation of linear momentum, which particle carries away the majority of the total kinetic energy liberated in the decay, and why?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Before Decay -->
  <g transform="translate(40, 20)">
    <circle cx="40" cy="65" r="26" fill="#f87171" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="18" y="70" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#7f1d1d">²²⁶₈₈Ra</text>
    <text x="14" y="110" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#475569">At Rest (p = 0)</text>
  </g>
  <line x1="120" y1="85" x2="160" y2="85" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="165,85 157,81 157,89" fill="#64748b"/>
  <!-- After Decay -->
  <g transform="translate(180, 20)">
    <!-- Daughter Radon recoils left -->
    <circle cx="45" cy="65" r="23" fill="#60a5fa" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="24" y="70" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#1e3a8a">²²²₈₆Rn</text>
    <line x1="20" y1="65" x2="-10" y2="65" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <polygon points="-15,65 -7,61 -7,69" fill="#1d4ed8"/>
    <text x="-15" y="55" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1d4ed8">v_Rn (recoil)</text>
    <!-- Alpha particle flies right -->
    <circle cx="120" cy="65" r="9" fill="#fbbf24" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="114" y="68" font-size="9" font-weight="800" fill="#78350f">α</text>
    <line x1="130" y1="65" x2="165" y2="65" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <polygon points="170,65 162,61 162,69" fill="#d97706"/>
    <text x="135" y="55" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#d97706">v_α (high)</text>
  </g>
</svg>

options.text: The alpha particle carries roughly 98.2% of the kinetic energy because K = p² / (2m), and the alpha particle has a vastly smaller mass (4 u vs 222 u).
The Radon daughter nucleus carries 98.2% of the kinetic energy because it is much heavier.
Both particles share the kinetic energy equally (50% each) due to Newton's third law.
All kinetic energy is converted into gamma photons with zero particle motion.

explanation:
Initial momentum is zero, so by conservation of linear momentum: p_α = -p_Rn, meaning both have equal magnitude of momentum p.
Kinetic energy is K = p² / (2m).
Therefore, K_α / K_Rn = m_Rn / m_α = 222 / 4 = 55.5.
The fraction of total kinetic energy carried by the alpha particle is:
K_α / K_total = m_Rn / (m_Rn + m_α) = 222 / 226 ≈ 98.2%.
The heavy daughter nucleus recoils with only ~1.8% of the decay energy.
concept_name: Momentum and Kinetic Energy Partition in Alpha Decay

title: Continuous Energy Spectrum of Beta Particles vs Alpha Line Spectrum
question: The graph compares the kinetic energy distribution of emitted alpha particles versus beta particles from radioactive nuclei. Why do alpha particles exhibit sharp, discrete energy lines, whereas beta particles show a continuous energy distribution ending at an endpoint energy E_max?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Axes -->
  <line x1="50" y1="170" x2="330" y2="170" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="330,170 322,166 322,174" fill="#334155"/>
  <text x="160" y="192" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Kinetic Energy (E) →</text>
  <line x1="50" y1="170" x2="50" y2="20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
  <polygon points="50,20 46,28 54,28" fill="#334155"/>
  <text x="14" y="115" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#334155" transform="rotate(-90,14,115)">Number of Particles →</text>
  <!-- Alpha sharp line -->
  <line x1="180" y1="170" x2="180" y2="35" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/>
  <circle cx="180" cy="35" r="4" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <text x="150" y="28" font-size="10" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626">α Line Spectrum (Discrete)</text>
  <!-- Beta continuous curve -->
  <path d="M 55 170 Q 110 50 160 80 T 260 170" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text x="80" y="70" font-size="10" font-weight="800" fill="#2563eb">β Continuous Spectrum</text>
  <text x="250" y="165" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">E_max</text>
</svg>

options.text: In beta decay, the decay energy is shared unpredictably between the beta particle and an antineutrino (three-body decay), whereas alpha decay is a two-body decay.
Beta particles lose energy randomly by colliding with inner orbital electrons before leaving the atom.
Alpha particles travel at variable speeds depending on ambient room temperature.
Beta particles are waves rather than material particles.

explanation:
Alpha decay is a two-body decay (Parent → Daughter + α), so conservation of momentum and energy uniquely fixes the kinetic energy of the alpha particle at a single discrete value.
In beta decay (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄), a third particle—the antineutrino (ν̄)—is simultaneously emitted (three-body decay). The available decay energy is continuously partitioned between the beta particle and the antineutrino, resulting in a continuous spectrum from 0 to E_max.
concept_name: Continuous Beta Spectrum and Antineutrino Hypothesis

title: Fractional Half-Life Decay Ladder
question: A radioisotope sample begins with mass M₀ = 48 g. The diagram displays the stepwise reduction of remaining active mass across consecutive half-lives (n = 1, 2, 3, 4). What is the remaining undecayed mass at stage n = 4, and what percentage of the original sample has decayed?
