  <rect x="160" y="127" width="40" height="33" fill="#3b82f6" rx="2"/>

  <text x="170" y="175" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#475569">n = 2</text>

  <text x="232" y="138" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1e3a8a">6 g</text>
  <text x="235" y="175" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#475569">n = 3</text>
  <!-- n = 4 -->
  <rect x="290" y="152" width="40" height="8" fill="#ef4444" rx="2"/>
  <text x="295" y="146" font-size="10" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626">?</text>
  <text x="300" y="175" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#475569">n = 4</text>

options.text: Remaining mass = 3.0 g; 93.75% has decayed
Remaining mass = 1.5 g; 96.88% has decayed
Remaining mass = 6.0 g; 87.50% has decayed
Remaining mass = 4.0 g; 91.67% has decayed

explanation:
At each half-life stage n, remaining mass M = M₀ × (1/2)ⁿ.
For n = 4:
M = 48 × (1/2)⁴ = 48 / 16 = 3.0 g.
Decayed mass = 48 - 3 = 45 g.
Percentage decayed = (45 / 48) × 100% = 93.75% (or 100% - (100% / 16) = 93.75%).

title: Comparing Curvature Radii in a Magnetic Chamber
question: In a cloud chamber subjected to a magnetic field, the radius of circular curvature r of a charged particle is governed by r = mv / (qB). Why is the radius of circular curvature for an alpha particle track significantly LARGER than that of a beta particle track of comparable kinetic energy?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 360 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fffcf7" rx="8"/>
  <!-- Gentle wide curve of Alpha -->
  <path d="M 60 160 A 180 180 0 0 1 200 30" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/>
  <text x="130" y="70" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">Alpha Track (Large r_α)</text>
  <!-- Sharp tight spiral/circle of Beta -->
  <circle cx="280" cy="110" r="32" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <text x="245" y="160" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">Beta Track (Small r_β)</text>
</svg>

options.text: Alpha particles possess vastly greater momentum p = √(2mK) due to their 7340-fold greater mass, yielding a much larger orbit radius r = p / (qB).
Alpha particles have no electric charge, so their radius is infinite.
The magnetic field selectively repels beta particles more strongly.
Beta particles travel faster than light in the chamber.

explanation:
Radius of circular path in magnetic field is r = p / (qB) = √(2mK) / (qB).
For comparable kinetic energies K, the ratio of radii is:
r_α / r_β = (√(m_α) / q_α) / (√(m_β) / q_β) = (√(7340 m_e) / 2e) / (√(m_e) / e) = (√7340) / 2 ≈ 85.7 / 2 ≈ 43.
Because the alpha particle's huge mass gives it vastly greater momentum for the same kinetic energy, its trajectory is much straighter (much larger radius of curvature r_α).
concept_name: Radius of Curvature in Magnetic Cloud Chambers

title: Nuclear Fusion Reaction of Deuterium and Tritium
question: The diagram depicts the D-T nuclear fusion reaction occurring in stellar cores and thermonuclear reactors: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV Why does this reaction require an extreme initial temperature of over 10⁷ K to initiate?

  <circle cx="180" cy="85" r="18" fill="#fbbf24" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="170" y="89" font-size="10" font-weight="800" fill="#78350f">Fusion</text>

  <line x1="205" y1="85" x2="255" y2="55" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/>

  <line x1="205" y1="85" x2="255" y2="115" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/>
  <circle cx="275" cy="120" r="8" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="268" y="123" font-size="8" font-weight="800" fill="#1e3a8a">¹₀n</text>
  <text x="235" y="165" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626">+ 17.6 MeV</text>

options.text: Positively charged nuclei experience strong electrostatic (Coulomb) repulsion; extreme thermal kinetic energy is required to overcome this barrier and bring them within nuclear force range (~10⁻¹⁵ m).
High temperature is needed to strip electrons so that nuclear fission can occur.
Deuterium and Tritium only exist as liquids below 10⁷ K.
High temperature converts the neutron into a proton.

explanation: Both Deuterium and Tritium nuclei carry positive charge (+1e). According to Coulomb's Law, as they approach each other, repulsive electrostatic force rises sharply. To overcome this Coulomb barrier and approach within ~10⁻¹⁵ m (where attractive strong nuclear forces dominate), the nuclei must possess enormous kinetic energy. This kinetic energy can only be achieved at temperatures exceeding 10⁷ to 10⁸ K (thermonuclear conditions).

title: Radioactivity as a Pure Nuclear Phenomenon
question: Why cannot radioactivity be altered, accelerated, or suppressed by physical factors (such as extreme temperature or pressure) or chemical changes (such as oxidation or compound formation)?

options.text: Radioactivity originates strictly from the instability of the atomic nucleus, whereas physical and chemical changes involve only the outermost valence electrons.
Physical and chemical changes have activation energies comparable to nuclear binding forces.
The nucleus is shielded by a vacuum that blocks all thermal heat transfer.
Radioactive elements cannot form chemical compounds.

explanation: Chemical reactions and physical state changes involve electron rearrangements in the outermost atomic shells with energies on the order of a few electron-volts (eV). Radioactivity, however, is a nuclear disintegration occurring deep within the nucleus governed by the strong nuclear force with binding energies on the order of mega-electron-volts (MeV, ~10⁶ times larger). Hence, chemical bonding, temperature, pressure, or magnetic fields have zero effect on nuclear decay rates.
concept_name: Nuclear Independence from Physical and Chemical States

title: Origin of Beta Particles from Inside the Nucleus
question: Since an atomic nucleus contains only protons and neutrons and NO orbital electrons, explain the exact nuclear transformation that produces an emitted beta (β⁻) particle.

options.text: A nuclear neutron spontaneously transforms into a proton, an electron (beta particle), and an antineutrino: ¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄.
An orbital K-shell electron falls into the nucleus and is immediately reflected out.
A proton splits into a neutron and an electron.
Two alpha particles collide inside the nucleus and emit an electron.

explanation:
In a neutron-rich unstable nucleus, a neutron spontaneously converts into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino:
¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄
The newly created proton remains bound inside the nucleus (increasing the atomic number Z by 1), while the fast-moving electron (β⁻ particle) cannot remain confined due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and is instantaneously expelled at high speed.
concept_name: Mechanism of Beta Decay in the Nucleus

title: Comparison of Ionizing Power Among Radiations
question: The ionizing powers of α, β, and γ radiations stand in the approximate ratio of 10,000: 100: 1. Why do alpha particles possess such immensely superior ionizing power compared to beta particles and gamma rays?

options.text: Alpha particles have the largest charge (+2e), greatest mass (4 u), and move relatively slowly (~10⁷ m/s), maximizing electrostatic interaction time with gas atoms.
Alpha particles travel at the speed of light, smashing atoms violently.
Alpha particles are uncharged and therefore can enter atomic electron clouds without repulsion.
Gamma rays have mass that neutralizes ionization.

explanation: Ionization occurs when radiation exerts Coulomb forces on orbital electrons to knock them out of atoms. Alpha particles have twice the elementary charge (+2e) and are ~7340 times heavier than electrons. Because they move relatively slowly (~5-7% of c), they spend more transit time near atoms, exerting massive electrostatic attraction on orbital electrons and creating up to 10,000 ion pairs per millimeter of track in air.
concept_name: Ionizing Power Mechanism of Alpha, Beta, and Gamma

title: Biological Hazards: Internal Ingestion vs External Exposure
question: Why is an alpha-emitting radioactive substance relatively harmless when kept outside the human body, but exceedingly lethal if inhaled or ingested?

options.text: Externally, alpha particles cannot penetrate the dead outer epidermal skin layer; internally, their high ionizing power causes intense localized cellular destruction and DNA damage.
Alpha particles react chemically with stomach acid to form hydrochloric acid gas.
Alpha particles become beta particles once inside living cells.
Body heat accelerates alpha particles to the speed of light.

explanation: Alpha particles have very low penetrating power (~0.04 mm in tissue) and are stopped completely by the dead cornified outer layer of the skin (stratum corneum). Outside the body, they pose virtually no hazard to living cells. However, if ingested or inhaled into the lungs, there is no dead protective skin barrier: the alpha particles directly irradiate living epithelial cells with their massive ionizing power (10,000x of gamma), causing severe double-strand DNA breaks and cancer.
concept_name: Biological Effects and Radiotoxicity of Alpha Radiations

title: Nuclear Change vs Chemical Change Distinctions
question: Which of the following fundamental statements highlights the essential difference between a nuclear reaction and a chemical reaction?

options.text: In a chemical reaction, atomic nuclei remain completely unchanged and elements conserve their identities; in a nuclear reaction, the nucleus itself changes, creating new elements through transmutation.
Chemical reactions release mega-electron-volts while nuclear reactions release electron-volts.
Mass is strictly conserved in nuclear reactions, but violated in chemical reactions.
Nuclear reactions depend strongly on room temperature and pressure.

explanation: In chemical reactions, atoms only rearrange their valence electron bonds; the atomic numbers Z and mass numbers A remain intact. In nuclear reactions (such as alpha decay, beta decay, or fission), the composition of the nucleus changes (transmutation of elements), and measurable mass defect Δm is converted into energy according to E = Δm · c².
concept_name: Fundamental Contrast Between Nuclear and Chemical Reactions

title: Sources and Nature of Background Radiation
question: Even when all radioactive sources are removed from a physics laboratory, a GM counter continues to register a steady count rate (e.g. 20-30 counts/min). What accounts for this background radiation?

options.text: Cosmic rays from outer space and naturally occurring terrestrial radioisotopes (such as Radon-222, Potassium-40, and Carbon-14 in rocks, building materials, and living tissue).
Static electricity generated by air conditioning currents.
Fluorescent tube lighting leaking electrons into the detector.
Microwave signals emitted from mobile phone towers.

explanation:
Background radiation is the omnipresent ionizing radiation in the natural environment. It arises from two primary sources:
1. Cosmic rays: high-energy muons and photons penetrating the upper atmosphere from outer space.
2. Terrestrial sources: radioactive radon gas (²²²Rn) emanating from ground soil/rocks, traces of Potassium-40 (⁴⁰K) and Carbon-14 (¹⁴C) naturally present in building stone and inside all organic tissue.

title: Radiation Safety Protocols and Waste Disposal
question: Which of the following constitutes the internationally recognized, safest protocol for disposing of high-level radioactive nuclear waste?

options.text: Vitrifying the waste into borosilicate glass blocks, sealing them in thick lead-lined stainless steel casks, and entombing them in deep geological repositories deep underground in stable rock formations.
Dumping into open ocean trenches inside ordinary plastic drums.
Incinerating the radioactive materials at high temperature in industrial furnaces.
Dissolving in strong acid and flushing into municipal drainage systems.

explanation: High-level radioactive waste remains active for thousands of years. It must be converted into an insoluble glass matrix (vitrification), sealed inside corrosion-resistant multi-barrier casks (lead and stainless steel), and stored in deep geological repositories (~500 m underground in stable tectonic bedrock) far away from groundwater tables and seismic fault zones.
concept_name: Radioactive Waste Management and Safety Precautions

title: Why Gamma Emission Causes No Change in A or Z
question: When a nucleus emits a gamma (γ) ray photon, its mass number A and atomic number Z remain strictly unchanged. What is the fundamental physical nature of gamma emission?

options.text: It is an electromagnetic transition where an excited daughter nucleus drops from an excited nuclear energy state to its ground state, dissipating surplus energy as a high-energy photon.
A proton converts into an antiproton, cancelling out charge.
Two neutrons fuse into a proton inside the core.
The nucleus absorbs an electron from outer shells.

explanation: Following alpha or beta decay, the daughter nucleus is often left in an excited nuclear energy level (denoted as X*). Just as an excited atom emits visible/UV photons when orbital electrons drop to lower orbits, an excited nucleus transitions to a lower energy state or ground state by emitting a gamma-ray photon (hν). Because photons have zero rest mass and zero electrical charge, neither A nor Z is altered: ᴬ_Z X* → ᴬ_Z X + γ.

title: Applications of Radioisotopes in Medicine and Archaeology
question: Match the correct radioisotope to its recognized medical or scientific application: 1. Cobalt-60 (⁶⁰Co) 2. Iodine-131 (¹³¹I) 3. Carbon-14 (¹⁴C) 4. Sodium-24 (²⁴Na)

options.text: ⁶⁰Co for cancer radiotherapy; ¹³¹I for thyroid diagnosis/treatment; ¹⁴C for carbon dating of fossils; ²⁴Na for tracing blood circulation and clots.
⁶⁰Co for carbon dating; ¹³¹I for blood circulation; ¹⁴C for cancer radiotherapy; ²⁴Na for thyroid treatment.
⁶⁰Co for smoke detectors; ¹³¹I for dating fossils; ¹⁴C for blood circulation; ²⁴Na for nuclear power.
All four are used exclusively as fuel in nuclear reactors.

explanation: Cobalt-60 emits penetrative gamma rays used in teletherapy to destroy cancer tumors. Iodine-131 is selectively absorbed by the thyroid gland and used for diagnosing and treating thyroid disorders. Carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years) is used in radiocarbon dating of once-living organic remains. Sodium-24 is an injected medical tracer used to detect blood clots and examine circulation efficiency.
concept_name: Radioisotope Applications in Medicine and Industry

title: Nuclear Forces vs Electrostatic Repulsion in Heavy Nuclei
question: Why do atomic nuclei with atomic number Z > 82 (such as Lead and Uranium) become naturally radioactive and unstable?

options.text: The short-range strong nuclear attraction (~10⁻¹⁵ m) acts only between nearest neighbors, while long-range electrostatic Coulomb repulsion between all protons across the large nucleus overcomes the nuclear binding force.
Heavy nuclei have too many electrons orbiting inside the nucleus.
The speed of neutrons inside heavy nuclei exceeds the speed of light.
Heavy elements absorb all cosmic rays from the atmosphere.

explanation: The strong nuclear force is extremely powerful but strictly short-range (~1 to 2 fm), saturating with nearest neighbor nucleons. In contrast, electrostatic Coulomb repulsion between positively charged protons is long-range (1/r²) and acts across the entire volume of the nucleus. In large nuclei (Z > 82), the cumulative electrostatic repulsion of dozens of protons exceeds the cohesive hold of nuclear forces, rendering the nucleus inherently unstable and radioactive.
concept_name: Nuclear Force Saturation and Radioactive Instability

title: Complete Decay Chain: Uranium-238 to Lead-206
question: A Uranium nucleus ²³⁸₉₂U undergoes a successive series of radioactive decays to eventually form a stable Lead nucleus ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + n_α (⁴₂He) + n_β (⁰₋₁e) Calculate the exact number of alpha particles (n_α) and beta particles (n_β) emitted in this decay series.
explanation:
1. Only alpha emissions alter the mass number A (each α reduces A by 4):
Total change in A = 238 - 206 = 32.
Number of α-particles n_α = 32 / 4 = 8.

2. Conservation of atomic number Z:
Initial Z = 92, Final Z = 82.
Change in Z = 92 - 82 = 10.
Each α reduces Z by 2; each β⁻ increases Z by 1:
2(n_α) - n_β = 10
2(8) - n_β = 10 ⟹ 16 - n_β = 10 ⟹ n_β = 6.

Therefore, 8 alpha particles and 6 beta particles are emitted.

title: Thorium Series Disintegration: Thorium-232 to Lead-208
question: The radioactive Thorium series begins with ²³²₉₀Th and terminates at stable ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. In another decay step, an intermediate nucleus ²²⁸₈₈Ra emits a beta particle to produce Actinium (Ac). Find the total number of alpha and beta particles emitted in the full Thorium series, and write the symbol with Z and A for the Actinium nucleus.

options.text: 6 α and 4 β; Actinium nucleus is ²²⁸₈₉Ac
8 α and 6 β; Actinium nucleus is ²²⁸₈₇Ac
6 α and 2 β; Actinium nucleus is ²²⁴₈₉Ac
4 α and 6 β; Actinium nucleus is ²³²₉₁Ac

explanation:
Change in mass number ΔA = 232 - 208 = 24 ⟹ n_α = 24 / 4 = 6 α-particles.
Change in atomic number ΔZ = 90 - 82 = 8.
Since 2(n_α) - n_β = 8 ⟹ 2(6) - n_β = 8 ⟹ 12 - n_β = 8 ⟹ n_β = 4 β-particles.
For the intermediate beta emission: ²²⁸₈₈Ra → ²²⁸₈₉Ac + ⁰₋₁e.
Mass number A remains 228, atomic number Z increases from 88 to 89: ²²⁸₈₉Ac.
concept_name: Thorium Decay Series and Intermediate Isotope Tracking

title: Geological Dating from Daughter-to-Parent Ratio
question: Analysis of a lunar rock specimen shows that the ratio of Lead-206 atoms to Uranium-238 atoms is 3: 1 (i.e. N_Pb / N_U = 3). Assuming no Lead was initially present when the rock solidified and that Uranium-238 decays with a half-life of 4.5 × 10⁹ years, what is the age of the rock?

options.text: 9.0 × 10⁹ years (2 half-lives)
1.35 × 10¹⁰ years (3 half-lives)
4.5 × 10⁹ years (1 half-life)
2.25 × 10⁹ years (0.5 half-life)

explanation:
Let the current number of Uranium atoms be N_U = 1 unit.
Then Lead atoms N_Pb = 3 units.
The initial number of Uranium atoms at solidification was N₀ = N_U + N_Pb = 1 + 3 = 4 units.
The fraction of original Uranium remaining is N_U / N₀ = 1 / 4 = (1/2)².
This means exactly n = 2 half-lives have elapsed.
Age of rock = 2 × T₁/₂ = 2 × (4.5 × 10⁹ years) = 9.0 × 10⁹ years.

title: Branching Decay and Isobar vs Isotope Relationship
question: Nucleus X(Z, A) emits an alpha particle to form nucleus Y. In a separate decay pathway, nucleus X emits two consecutive beta particles to form nucleus W. In a third pathway, nucleus Y emits one beta particle to form nucleus Z. Which pair among X, Y, W, and Z are ISOBARS (same mass number, different atomic number)?

options.text: X and W are isobars (both have mass number A)
X and Y are isobars
Y and W are isobars
W and Z are isobars

explanation:
Let original nucleus be ᴬ_Z X.
1. X emits α ⟹ Y has mass number A-4 and atomic number Z-2: ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z-2} Y.
2. X emits two β⁻ particles ⟹ each β⁻ leaves mass number unchanged but increases Z by 1. Thus W has mass number A and atomic number Z+2: ᴬ_{Z+2} W.
Because X and W both have the EXACT same mass number A, but different atomic numbers (Z vs Z+2), X and W are by definition ISOBARS.

title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy per Nucleon of Helium-4
question: Given: Mass of proton m_p = 1.00728 u, mass of neutron m_n = 1.00866 u, and measured mass of Helium-4 nucleus m_α = 4.00150 u. (1 u = 931.5 MeV). Calculate the mass defect Δm of the Helium-4 nucleus and its binding energy per nucleon.

options.text: Δm = 0.03038 u; B.E. per nucleon ≈ 7.07 MeV
Δm = 0.04520 u; B.E. per nucleon ≈ 10.5 MeV
Δm = 0.01519 u; B.E. per nucleon ≈ 3.54 MeV
Δm = 0.06076 u; B.E. per nucleon ≈ 14.15 MeV

explanation:
A Helium-4 nucleus contains Z = 2 protons and (A - Z) = 2 neutrons.
Total mass of constituent nucleons:
2(m_p) + 2(m_n) = 2(1.00728) + 2(1.00866) = 2.01456 + 2.01732 = 4.03188 u.
Mass defect Δm = 4.03188 - 4.00150 = 0.03038 u.
Total binding energy E_b = 0.03038 × 931.5 MeV = 28.299 MeV.
Binding energy per nucleon = E_b / A = 28.299 / 4 ≈ 7.07 MeV/nucleon.
concept_name: Mass Defect and Binding Energy Calculation

title: Energy Liberated from Complete Fission of 1 kg Uranium-235
question: Assuming each fission of Uranium-235 releases 200 MeV of energy, calculate the total energy in Joules liberated by the complete fission of 1.0 kg of pure Uranium-235. (Avogadro's number N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).

options.text: 8.21 × 10¹³ J (equivalent to burning ~2,500 tonnes of high-grade coal)

explanation:
1. Number of moles in 1 kg (1000 g) of ²³⁵U = 1000 / 235 ≈ 4.255 mol.
2. Total number of nuclei N = 4.255 × 6.02 × 10²³ ≈ 2.562 × 10²⁴ nuclei.
3. Total energy in MeV = 2.562 × 10²⁴ × 200 MeV = 5.124 × 10²⁶ MeV.
4. Converting to Joules:
Total Energy = 5.124 × 10²⁶ × (10⁶) × (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) ≈ 8.21 × 10¹³ J.
This demonstrates the staggering energy density of nuclear fission compared to fossil fuels.
concept_name: Total Energy Release in Complete Fission

title: Crossed Fields Velocity Selector for Beta Beam
question: A beam of beta particles enters a region containing mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields (E = 6.0 × 10⁴ V/m directed downward, B = 0.20 T directed into the page). At what exact velocity v must the beta particles travel so that the electric force exactly cancels the magnetic force, allowing them to pass through completely undeflected?

options.text: 3.0 × 10⁵ m/s (using v = E / B)

explanation:
For zero net deflection, the electric force F_e = qE must equal the magnetic Lorentz force F_b = qvB in magnitude:
qE = qvB
Canceling charge q gives:
v = E / B = (6.0 × 10⁴ V/m) / (0.20 T) = 3.0 × 10⁵ m/s.
Beta particles with this exact velocity continue straight ahead along the central axis, while all other speeds are deflected away.
concept_name: Velocity Selector in Crossed E and B Fields

title: Sequential Decay Yielding an Isotope of the Ancestor
question: A radioactive nucleus X emits one alpha particle followed by two beta particles in successive disintegrations: X → Y + α; Y → Z + β⁻; Z → W + β⁻. What is the relationship between the final daughter nucleus W and the original ancestor nucleus X?

options.text: W is an isotope of X (same atomic number Z, but mass number A is 4 units less)
W is an isobar of X (same mass number A)
W is identical in all respects to X
W has atomic number Z+2 and mass number A

explanation:
Let original ancestor be ᴬ_Z X.
1. Alpha decay: ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z-2} Y + ⁴₂He.
2. First beta decay: ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z-2} Y → ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z-1} Z + ⁰₋₁e.
3. Second beta decay: ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z-1} Z → ᴬ⁻⁴_Z W + ⁰₋₁e.
Comparing W and X:
Both have the EXACT same atomic number Z, which means they belong to the same chemical element.
However, W has mass number (A - 4), which is 4 units less than X.
Therefore, W is an ISOTOPE of X.
concept_name: Isotope Generation Through Alpha Followed by Two Betas

title: Half-Life Mass Calculation After Elapsed Time
question: The half-life of a radioactive isotope Sodium-24 (²⁴Na) is 15 hours. If a clinic receives an initial mass of 64.0 mg, what mass of Sodium-24 remains undecayed after exactly 60 hours?

options.text: 4.0 mg
8.0 mg
2.0 mg

explanation:
1. Half-life T₁/₂ = 15 hours.
2. Total elapsed time t = 60 hours.
3. Number of elapsed half-lives n = t / T₁/₂ = 60 / 15 = 4.
4. Remaining mass M = M₀ × (1/2)ⁿ = 64.0 × (1/2)⁴ = 64.0 / 16 = 4.0 mg.

title: Activity Count Rate Reduction Across Multiple Half-Lives
question: A freshly isolated radioactive tracer sample exhibits an initial activity of 1600 Bq. What will its activity be after 4 complete half-lives have elapsed?

options.text: 100 Bq
200 Bq
400 Bq
50 Bq

explanation:
Activity after n half-lives is given by A = A₀ × (1/2)ⁿ.
Here A₀ = 1600 Bq and n = 4.
A = 1600 × (1/2)⁴ = 1600 / 16 = 100 Bq.

title: Energy Equivalent of Mass Defect in Atomic Mass Units
question: During a nuclear disintegration, a mass defect of Δm = 0.050 amu is observed. Given that 1 amu is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy, calculate the energy released in MeV.
explanation:
Energy released E = Δm × 931.5 MeV/amu.
E = 0.050 × 931.5 = 46.575 MeV.
concept_name: Mass-Energy Conversion in Atomic Mass Units

title: Time Required for Fractional Disintegration
question: A radioactive element has a half-life of 20 days. In what total time will exactly 87.5% of the original sample have disintegrated?

options.text: 60 days (3 half-lives)
40 days (2 half-lives)
80 days (4 half-lives)
100 days (5 half-lives)

explanation:
1. If 87.5% of the sample has decayed, the remaining fraction is:
Remaining = 100% - 87.5% = 12.5% = 1/8 of original.
2. Since (1/2)ⁿ = 1/8 = (1/2)³, exactly n = 3 half-lives have elapsed.
3. Total time t = n × T₁/₂ = 3 × 20 days = 60 days.

title: Alpha Particle Kinetic Energy Percentage
question: A stationary Radium-226 nucleus decays into Radon-222 by emitting an alpha particle: ²²⁶Ra → ²²²Rn + ⁴He. If the total disintegration energy Q is 4.87 MeV, what is the kinetic energy of the emitted alpha particle?

options.text: 2.44 MeV (50% of Q)

explanation:
By conservation of momentum and energy:
K_α = Q × (m_Rn / (m_Rn + m_α)) = 4.87 × (222 / 226) = 4.87 × 0.9823 ≈ 4.78 MeV.
The recoiling daughter nucleus takes only 4.87 - 4.78 = 0.09 MeV.
concept_name: Kinetic Energy of Emitted Alpha Particle

title: Count Rate with Background Radiation Subtraction Trap
question: A Geiger-Müller counter records a steady background radiation rate of 25 counts/min. When a radioactive sample is introduced, the total measured count rate rises to 425 counts/min. If the sample has a half-life of 3 hours, what will the TOTAL measured count rate on the counter be after 6 hours?

options.text: 125 counts/min (100 counts/min source + 25 counts/min background)
106.25 counts/min
100 counts/min
212.5 counts/min

explanation:
1. The TRUE net count rate of the radioactive source at t = 0 is:
Net R₀ = Measured Rate - Background = 425 - 25 = 400 counts/min.
2. In t = 6 hours, number of half-lives n = 6 / 3 = 2 half-lives.
3. Net count rate of source after 2 half-lives = 400 / 2² = 400 / 4 = 100 counts/min.
4. The detector continuously registers background radiation, so the total measured count rate will be:
Total Measured = Net Source + Background = 100 + 25 = 125 counts/min.
(Note: Option B is the classic trap of simply dividing 425 by 4 without subtracting background first!).
concept_name: Background Radiation Subtraction in Count Rate

title: Mass Defect from Einstein's Mass-Energy Equation in SI Units
question: Using Einstein's mass-energy equation E = Δm · c² (where c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), determine the mass defect in kilograms required to generate exactly 9.0 × 10¹³ Joules of energy.

options.text: 1.0 kg

explanation:
From E = Δm · c²:
Δm = E / c² = (9.0 × 10¹³ J) / (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)² = (9.0 × 10¹³) / (9.0 × 10¹⁶) = 1.0 × 10⁻³ kg = 1.0 g.
Thus, converting just one gram of matter entirely into energy yields a colossal 90 trillion Joules.
concept_name: Einstein Mass-Energy Conversion in SI Units
